displayQuote: Nothing is more powerful than an idea whose time has come

meta.title: Who really said "Nothing is more powerful than an idea whose time has come"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Victor Hugo. The saying grew out of Émile Souvestre (1848) and Gustave Aimard (1861). Hugo's real 1877 line is about resisting an invasion of ideas.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nothing is more powerful than an idea whose time has come'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Victor Hugo. The earliest known form is Émile Souvestre's, from 1848. Hugo's real 1877 line says an invasion of ideas cannot be resisted.

answer.label: Not Victor Hugo — earliest known form is Émile Souvestre’s
answer.sourceLine: The earliest form Quote Investigator ↗ found is from Souvestre’s 1848 article in the Revue des deux mondes: “il y a quelque chose de plus puissant que la force, que le courage, que le génie même : c’est l’idée dont le temps est venu.” Hugo wrote only a related line, in 1877, about resisting an “invasion of ideas.” The English wording credited to him took shape in the 20th century.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: “La Chouannerie dans le Poitou: Le Sonneur de cloches”

source.excerpt:
Or, dans toute question humaine, il y a quelque chose de plus puissant que la force, que le courage, que le génie même : c’est l’idée dont le temps est venu.

“Now, in every human question, there is something more powerful than strength, than courage, than genius itself: it is the idea whose time has come.”
trail: Quote Investigator (5 Nov 2023) ↗ traces the family of sayings. It starts with Souvestre in 1848, then two 1861 novels by Gustave Aimard, then Hugo’s related 1877 line. Hugo is credited with the “idea whose time has come” wording from 1912 on.
Wikiquote’s Victor Hugo page ↗ lists “There is nothing more powerful than an idea whose time has come” as Misattributed. It notes the wording is closer to Aimard’s Les Francs-Tireurs (1861).
Hugo’s actual words, in the conclusion of Histoire d’un crime (French text on Wikisource ↗): “On résiste à l’invasion des armées ; on ne résiste pas à l’invasion des idées.”
In the T. H. Joyce and Arthur Locker English translation (Project Gutenberg ↗): “An invasion of armies can be resisted; an invasion of ideas cannot be resisted.”
source.excerptNote: French text and English translation as Quote Investigator gives them. The popular English wording, “Nothing is more powerful than an idea whose time has come,” does not appear in Souvestre’s article or in any work by Hugo.

source.rightsNote: Souvestre’s 1848 French text and Hugo’s 1877 Histoire d’un crime are long in the public domain. The popular English sentence, though, grew up anonymously in the 20th century with no single identifiable source, so we make no rights claim about this exact wording.

author.name: Émile Souvestre
author.heading: About the real source
author.bio: Émile Souvestre was a Breton novelist from Morlaix. He did better as a novelist and as a collector of Breton folklore (Le Foyer breton, 1844) than as a playwright. Un Philosophe sous les toits won an academic prize in 1851. In 1848 he wrote an article on the Chouannerie for the Revue des deux mondes. It contains the earliest known “idea whose time has come.”

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This saying belongs to a family of variants (“No army can stop an idea whose time has come,” “There is one thing stronger than all the armies in the world…”). They have been pinned on several famous names. None of these names goes with this wording.

items.why: Hugo’s nearest real line is from Histoire d’un crime (1877): “On résiste à l’invasion des armées ; on ne résiste pas à l’invasion des idées.” It says nothing about an idea “whose time has come.” Quote Investigator ↗ finds the Hugo credit for that phrase in a 1912 piece by Frederic C. Howe. It then spread through 1914 suffrage columns, Ralph Waldo Trine (1917) and a 1964 Container Corporation advertisement in Time. Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed.

Aimard’s 1861 novel Les francs tireurs has, in Frederic Wraxall’s English translation of the same year, “there is something more powerful than the brute force of bayonets: it is the idea whose time has come and hour struck.” His Les rodeurs de frontières (1861) closely echoes Souvestre. Both points are in Quote Investigator ↗.

Quote Investigator ↗ records a 1939 U.S. Senate subcommittee exhibit. In it, a National Industrial Council letter says: “Disraeli once said, ‘There is nothing in the world so powerful as an idea whose time has come.’” QI gives no source in Disraeli’s own writings.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest “idea whose time has come” that Quote Investigator ↗ found is Émile Souvestre’s, from 1848. QI believes the modern English versions evolved from these earlier lines. It recommends quoting the precise words with the correct author.

context.heading: How a French phrase became an American proverb
lead: Souvestre was writing about the Chouannerie, a royalist uprising in western France, and he expected the side he favored to win in the end. Gustave Aimard reused the phrase in two 1861 adventure novels, and those were translated into English that same year. Hugo’s own line, published in 1877, makes a different point: armies can be resisted, but ideas cannot.

In English the saying took off in the 20th century, with Hugo as its usual source. Quote Investigator ↗ finds it in women’s-suffrage writing of 1912 and 1914, in religious periodicals of 1917 and 1921, and in a 1964 Time advertisement from Container Corporation of America. That ad captioned the line “Victor Hugo, 1802-1885, The Future of Man.”
context.pull: An invasion of armies can be resisted; an invasion of ideas cannot be resisted. — Victor Hugo, 1877
